passages.t: Judah goes first, and a captured king's verdict
passages.happening:
Joshua is dead, and the book opens with a question to God. The Israelites ask the LORD, “Who will be the first to go up and fight for us against the Canaanites?” (verse 1). The answer comes at once: “Judah shall go up” (verse 2). God adds that he has already given the land into their hands.

Judah asks its neighbor tribe Simeon to fight beside it, and promises to help Simeon in turn (verse 3). At a place called Bezek they defeat the Canaanites and the Perizzites, two of the peoples of the land. The local king, Adoni-bezek, runs. They catch him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes (verses 4-6).

Then the captured king says what has happened to him. “Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off have gathered the scraps under my table. As I have done to them, so God has repaid me” (verse 7). He is taken to Jerusalem, and he dies there.
passages.hearers:
Under Joshua, Israel had one leader. Now it has none, and each tribe must take its own land. So the people go straight to God and ask. It is a good beginning. The rest of the book will show what happens as the asking fades.

Judah is sent first. Judah was the largest tribe in the south, and the line of King David would later come from it. Simeon's land lay inside Judah's, in the far south, so the two tribes fought together naturally. The Canaanites and Perizzites were among the peoples living in the land before Israel came.

Cutting off a captured king's thumbs and big toes left him unable to hold a weapon or to run into battle. It also shamed him in front of everyone. Adoni-bezek, whose name means lord of Bezek, had done this to seventy lesser kings, the rulers of small city-states, and made them scrabble for scraps under his table. Now it is done to him.

The narrator passes no comment. He lets the captured king speak, and the king reads his own fate as God's justice: what he did to others has been done to him. That is a true reading of his own life. It is not a command to Israel, and the scene is not held up as a pattern. The book is showing the cruelty of the age in which Israel lived, and which Israel often shared.
passages.later:
The rule Adoni-bezek states runs through the whole Bible. Jesus said, “For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged; and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you” (Matthew 7:2). Paul put it as a farmer would: “Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return” (Galatians 6:7).

Judah, sent first here, is the tribe from which David's royal line came. The letter to the Hebrews says, “For it is clear that our Lord descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14).
passages.hard:
Was Judah right to maim the king?

The text does not say. It reports what Judah did and then gives the last word to Adoni-bezek, who had done the same to seventy others and calls his own fate God's repayment. That is the verdict of a cruel man on himself. It is not a word from God to Israel, and nothing in the chapter makes it a model for how anyone should treat a prisoner.

Judges often works this way. It tells what happened, plainly, and leaves the reader to weigh it by what follows and by the law and the prophets. Here the reader is meant to feel two things at once: that the king's cruelty came back on his own head, and that the people of God are already living by the ways of the land around them.
passages.asks: The book opens with Israel asking God what to do. Ask how often your plans begin with asking him, and how often you ask only once you have already started. And hear the captured king: ‘As I have done to them, so God has repaid me’. Ask whether there is anything you are doing to others that you would not want done to you.

passages.t: Hebron, Acsah's springs, and the chariots of the plain
passages.happening:
Judah attacks Jerusalem, takes it, and sets it on fire (verse 8). Then Judah goes down to fight the Canaanites in the hill country, in the dry south called the Negev, and in the low hills toward the coast (verse 9). Judah takes Hebron (verse 10), and Caleb, to whom Moses had promised it, drives out the descendants of Anak there (verse 20).

Caleb offers his daughter Acsah in marriage to the man who takes the town of Debir. His nephew Othniel takes it, and marries her (verses 12-13). Acsah urges her husband to ask her father for a field. Then she rides to Caleb herself, and when she gets down from her donkey he asks what she wants. “Give me a blessing,” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” Caleb gives her the upper and the lower springs (verse 15).

The family of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenites, settle among the people of Judah in the south (verse 16). Judah and Simeon devote the town of Zephath to destruction, and it is renamed Hormah (verse 17). Judah takes Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron on the coast (verse 18).

Then the account turns. ‘The LORD was with Judah’, the writer says, and Judah took the hill country, “but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron” (verse 19). And Benjamin, Judah's neighbor to the north, fails to drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem: “So to this day the Jebusites live there among the Benjamites” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Some of this was already told in the book of Joshua: Hebron, Debir, Acsah's springs, and the Jebusites who stayed in Jerusalem. Judges gathers these old reports at the start of a new age, to show where things stood when Joshua died.

Jerusalem is a puzzle. Judah burns it in verse 8, yet in verse 21 the Jebusites still live there, and Israel did not hold the city until David took it many years later. Most scholars think Judah raided and burned it but could not keep it.

Acsah's scene is short, and it is the brightest moment in the chapter. Land in the Negev was nearly worthless without water. A daughter's marriage often came with a gift from her father, and she asks for the gift that will keep her household alive. She sees what is missing and goes to get it, plainly and boldly. In a chapter of failures she is a picture of what Israel could have been: a people who asked for what God meant them to have, and received it. Caleb's offer of his daughter to the man who took a town was a way of honoring a champion in that world. It is no pattern for today, and the writer spends his words on Acsah herself. Othniel, who marries her, will be the first of the judges (3:9).

The Kenites were a clan related to Moses' father-in-law. They came up from the City of Palms, which is Jericho, and lived among the people of Judah. A Kenite household will matter again in chapter 4.

Hormah comes from the same Hebrew root as the word for devoting a town to destruction, the ban described in Deuteronomy and Joshua. The name recalls an older vow made at the same place in the time of Moses. The book page and the notes on Joshua 6 set out how Christians have read the ban. They say plainly that no one may use these chapters to justify violence against any person or people, and that the peoples named here passed away long ago.

Verse 18 says that Judah took three cities on the coast that later belonged to the Philistines. The ancient Greek translation, called the Septuagint, reads the verse the other way, as saying that Judah did not take them.

Then come the iron chariots. A chariot was the fast and frightening weapon of the age, and it worked best on flat, open ground. Israel was a people of the hills, fighting on foot. The towns of the plains were strong, and the hill tribes could not take them.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua tells Acsah's story in nearly the same words (Joshua 15:16-19), and it admits the failure at Jerusalem in almost the same words as verse 21: “But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem” (Joshua 15:63).

Joshua had also told the tribes that chariots need not stop them: “Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out” (Joshua 17:18).

Jerusalem was finally taken by David: “Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)” (2 Samuel 5:7).

Hormah had first been named in the wilderness: “Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction; so they named the place Hormah” (Numbers 21:3).
passages.hard:
How can the LORD be with Judah, and Judah still not drive out the people with iron chariots?

The verse is uncomfortable, because it seems to say that God's presence was not enough. Readers have taken it in two ways.

Some read it as a plain report of war. Soldiers on foot from the hill country could not beat chariots on open plains, and the writer says so honestly.

Others remember that Joshua had promised the tribes they could drive out the Canaanites even though they had iron chariots (Joshua 17:18). They read verse 19 as quietly exposing a failure of trust, not a limit on God. The way the chapter slides toward failure, and God's rebuke at the start of chapter 2, support this second reading.

The first reading is also part of the picture. The narrator reports what Israel could not do, and the next chapter explains why.
passages.asks: Acsah saw that her land could not live without water, and she went and asked for it. Ask what you have been given that will not bear fruit without something more from God, and whether you have asked him plainly. Then look at verse 19. Ask where you have decided that something in your life is too strong to change, and whether that is a fact about it or about your trust.

passages.t: Bethel taken, and a list of towns not taken
passages.happening:
The house of Joseph, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, attacks Bethel, “and the LORD was with them” (verse 22). Their spies see a man coming out of the city and say, “Please show us how to get into the city, and we will treat you kindly” (verse 24). He shows them. They take the city and let him and his family go, and he goes to the land of the Hittites, builds a town, and names it Luz, the old name of Bethel (verses 25-26).

From there the chapter becomes a list. Manasseh does not drive out the people of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam and Megiddo, “for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land” (verse 27). When Israel grows stronger, it puts them to forced labor instead (verse 28). Ephraim does not drive out the people of Gezer (verse 29). Zebulun, Asher and Naphtali each fail in turn (verses 30-33).

Last of all, the tribe of Dan cannot even hold its own ground. “The Amorites forced the Danites into the hill country and did not allow them to come down into the plain” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Bethel was an old holy place. It was here that Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching up to heaven, and here that he renamed the town of Luz Bethel, which means house of God. Its capture comes by help from inside, as Jericho's did through Rahab. But the stories end differently. Rahab confessed Israel's God and came to live among Israel. This man does neither. He takes his family far away and builds a new Luz.

The list moves from south to north, and its tone darkens as it goes. Judah's section was mostly success. The northern tribes' sections are mostly failure. The key words change too: first ‘the LORD was with’ a tribe, then, again and again, a tribe ‘failed to drive out’ the people of a place.

Watch who lives among whom. First the Canaanites live among Israel (verse 29). Then Israel lives among the Canaanites (verse 32). Then Dan is pushed back altogether (verse 34). The chapter is describing a slide.

The cities named were not villages. Megiddo, Taanach, Beth-shean and Gezer were fortified Canaanite cities guarding the great valleys and trade roads, on open ground where chariots could fight. Beth-shean had been a base of Egyptian rule. Gezer did not become Israel's until a pharaoh captured it and gave it to Solomon as a dowry, generations later.

Forced labor meant that a conquered people were made to work for the stronger, building and farming. It was common in the ancient world. In the book's own terms it was a failure. The law had told Israel to make no treaty with the peoples of the land, so that their gods would not draw Israel away. Putting them to work looked like strength. It was a compromise that kept the danger close and added a second wrong.

Dan's failure has a long shadow. Pushed out of its land, Dan will go north to find another, and that story is told in chapter 18.
passages.later:
Joshua had warned the people what would happen if they lived among the nations that remained: “know for sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you. Instead, they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes” (Joshua 23:13). The next chapter of Judges repeats the warning as God's judgment.

The law's reason was the worship of other gods: “they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). A psalm looks back on these years and says that it happened: “They did not destroy the peoples as the LORD had commanded them, but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs. They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them” (Psalm 106:34-36).

Forced labor later came back on Israel's own head: “Then King Solomon conscripted a labor force of 30,000 men from all Israel” (1 Kings 5:13).
passages.hard:
Was it better to put the Canaanites to forced labor than to drive them out?

Within the book, no. The point of the list is failure. The tribes did not do what they had been told, and the next chapter says so in God's own words.

A reader today will see a second problem as well, and is right to. Forced labor is a wrong in itself. The book reports it and does not praise it, and Israel later learned its weight when its own king laid the same yoke on his people. These notes take the verses as a report of what the tribes did, and not as approval of it. Nothing here makes forced labor right.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The tribes did not refuse God outright. They settled for less, one town at a time, and called it strength. Ask where you have made a quiet arrangement with something God told you to be rid of, because keeping it was useful. Ask who pays for that arrangement. And ask what the next generation in your home or your church will inherit from the compromises you have made.
